articles.title: The Day Our AI Prompt Became a Monolith
articles.author: Dedipya Goswami
articles.description:
How we transformed a 10,000-line Salesforce AI assistant into a scalable agent architecture
How we transformed a 10,000-line Salesforce AI assistant into a sca...
articles.content:
How we transformed a 10,000-line Salesforce AI assistant into a scalable agent architecture

When I joined the team working on our Salesforce CPQ product, one of my assignments sounded fairly straightforward.

“Build an AI assistant that can help Salesforce administrators perform their daily work.”

Initially, that sounded like a typical chatbot.

Except… it wasn’t.

The assistant wasn’t supposed to answer questions.

It was supposed to do work.

Instead of searching documentation, it needed to understand an administrator’s intent and execute real business operations inside a Salesforce organization.

For example:

“Create a Discount Rule that applies 15% off for Gold customers.”

Or…

“Generate a Quote for Contoso Ltd.”

Or…

“Create a Product with three configurable Options.”

Or even…

“Create an Account and assign it to the North America Sales team.”

Instead of navigating through dozens of Salesforce pages, administrators could simply ask the chatbot.

The vision was simple:

Reduce manual administrative work using AI.

Version One: One Chatbot To Rule Them All

Our first implementation followed a very common pattern.

One chatbot. One system prompt. One brain.

Everything lived inside that prompt.

It contained:

  • Product creation guidelines
  • Quote generation rules
  • CPQ Rule creation workflows
  • Permission checks
  • Salesforce best practices
  • Business constraints
  • Output formatting
  • Safety guardrails
  • Tool usage instructions
  • Hundreds of examples

At first…

it worked surprisingly well.

Whenever a new feature was requested, we simply added another section to the prompt.

Need Quote generation?
↓
Add instructions.
↓
Need Product creation?
↓
Add instructions.
↓
Need another guardrail?
↓
Add another paragraph.

It felt productive.

Until it wasn’t.

The Prompt Started Looking Like Software

A few months later, I opened the system prompt. It wasn’t a prompt anymore.

It had quietly grown into nearly ten thousand lines of instructions.

Not ten thousand tokens.

Ten thousand lines.

And that’s when something clicked. The problem wasn’t prompt engineering. The problem was software architecture.

The prompt now contained things that normally belong inside applications:

  • Business logic
  • Workflow definitions
  • Validation rules
  • Security instructions
  • Permission handling
  • Exception cases
  • API usage
  • Examples
  • Routing logic

Somewhere along the way… we had accidentally built an application inside a text file.

The Symptoms

As the prompt grew, problems started appearing everywhere.

1. Every Feature Made Everything Harder

A request like:

“Support Bundle Products.”

didn’t only affect Product creation. It unexpectedly impacted Quote generation… Rule creation…Validation …Output formatting.

Because everything shared the same prompt.

2. Nobody Wanted To Touch It

Imagine opening a file like this.

system_prompt.md (9,842 lines)

Where do you insert a new instruction?

Will it conflict with another one?

Can something be removed safely?

Nobody knew anymore.

3. Testing Became Painful

A tiny wording change could unexpectedly affect an unrelated capability.

Changing Product instructions sometimes made Quote generation worse.

Updating Rule creation could influence Account creation.

The model had started treating everything as one enormous context.

4. Every Request Carried Thousands of Tokens

Even if the user only wanted:

“Create a Product.”

We were sending instructions about:

  • Quotes
  • Accounts
  • Pricing Rules
  • Documentation
  • Product Options
  • Validation
  • Security

Every single time.

That meant:

  • Higher latency
  • Higher token usage
  • Higher cost

The First Architectural Change

Instead of making one chatbot smarter…

we decided to make multiple chatbots smaller.

                    User
                     │
                     ▼
             Intent Detection
                     │
 ┌──────────┬────────┼─────────┬────────────┐
 ▼          ▼        ▼         ▼            ▼
Rule      Quote   Product   Account   Documentation
Agent      Agent     Agent      Agent        Agent

Each agent had exactly one responsibility.

The Rule Agent understood CPQ Rules.

The Quote Agent focused on Quotes and Opportunities

The Product Agent handled Products, Options and Option Groups.

The Account Agent managed Salesforce Accounts.

Each one had:

  • its own system prompt
  • its own tools
  • its own validation
  • its own examples

Suddenly everything became much easier.

Smaller prompts. Cleaner testing. Clear ownership. Independent deployments.

It felt like moving from a monolith to microservices.

Because that’s exactly what it was.

Then History Repeated Itself

A few months later…

The Product Agent started growing.

It now needed to know about:

  • Products
  • Option Groups
  • Product Options
  • Price Books
  • Pricing Rules
  • Validation Rules
  • Duplicate Detection
  • Permission Checks
  • Required Fields
  • Salesforce Object Relationships

Its prompt kept growing.

The Quote Agent did the same. The Rule Agent too.

We had solved one monolith.

Only to create several smaller monoliths.

That’s When We Stopped Thinking About Prompts

Instead…

I started thinking about architecture.

The question changed from:

“How do we write better prompts?”

to

“What actually belongs inside a prompt?”

That simple question changed how we approached the entire system.

Principle 1 — Prompts Should Describe Behavior

Bad Prompt :

↓
Contains:
• Pricing tables
• Salesforce schemas
• Field mappings
• Validation rules
• Product catalog

Good Prompt:

↓
You are responsible for creating Products.
↓
Use ProductService whenever product
information is required.

Principle 2 — Move Business Logic Into Code

This was probably the biggest improvement.

Instead of writing:

If Product Type is Bundle
AND PriceBook exists
AND User has Permission X
THEN...

inside the prompt…

the prompt simply called:

createProduct()
↓
Backend Validation
↓
Permission Check
↓
Duplicate Check
↓
Salesforce API

The model no longer needed to memorize business rules.

The backend guaranteed correctness.

I realized that we have got dependent on AI and giving it the work to do the validation instead of putting that in, in our code

Principle 3 — Inject Context Dynamically

One mistake we made early on was sending everything.

Instead of this:

Entire Documentation + Entire Prompt + Entire Conversation

we moved toward:

User Request
↓
Intent
↓
Relevant Context
↓
Relevant Documentation
↓
Relevant Tools
↓
LLM

If the user wanted to create a Quote…

there was no reason to include Product documentation.

The model only received what it needed.

Nothing more.

Principle 4 — Prompts Should Be Modular

Instead of maintaining:

system_prompt.md

we broke prompts into reusable modules.

identity.md
security.md
tool_usage.md
workflow.md
response_style.md
examples.md

At runtime, the system assembled only the modules required for the current task.

Very similar to importing software libraries.

Principle 5 — Build an Orchestrator

Instead of expecting one model to understand everything…

we introduced routing.

                   User
                     │
                     ▼
              Orchestrator
                     │
     ┌───────────────┼────────────────┐
     ▼               ▼                ▼
 Product Agent   Quote Agent     Rule Agent
     │               │                │
     ▼               ▼                ▼
 Product API     Quote API       Rule Engine

The orchestrator became responsible for choosing the right expert.

Each expert stayed focused.

Principle 6 — Treat Prompts Like Production Code

This was perhaps the biggest mindset shift. Prompts aren’t documentation. They’re production code. So they deserve the same engineering discipline.

That means:

  • Version control
  • Pull requests
  • Code reviews
  • Regression tests
  • Change logs
  • Ownership

The more important your AI system becomes…

the less your prompts should resemble notes in a text editor.

Looking Back

When we started, I thought prompt engineering was mostly about writing better instructions.

Now I see it differently.

Large prompts aren’t the problem.

Prompts that contain application logic are.

The moment a prompt starts replacing software, it’s usually a signal that the architecture needs to evolve.

Breaking one chatbot into specialized agents was only the first step.

The real lesson was learning where prompts should end, and where software engineering should begin.

articles.title: I Thought ChatGPT and the OpenAI API Were the Same. I Was Wrong.
articles.author: Dedipya Goswami
articles.description:

articles.content:
A few days ago, I was building an AI feature for one of my projects.

Like many developers, I already had an OpenAI API key, so my assumption was simple:

“If ChatGPT is powered by GPT-5.5, and my API also gives me GPT-5.5, then both should behave exactly the same.”

That sounded logical.

So I started testing.

First, I asked ChatGPT a question about a recent AI release. It searched the web, cited fresh sources, and returned a detailed answer that felt almost like it had researched the topic for me.

Then I copied the exact same prompt into my application that was using the OpenAI API.

The response wasn’t bad.

It just wasn’t… the same.

There were no web results.

No recent information.

No intelligent decision to search.

No additional context.

At first, I thought I had configured something incorrectly.

Maybe I had forgotten a parameter.

Maybe there was a hidden setting.

Maybe ChatGPT had some secret prompt that I didn’t.

After spending nearly an hour reading documentation and experimenting, I realized something that completely changed the way I think about modern AI systems.

The difference wasn’t the model.

The difference was everything around the model.

The Question That Started It All

The more I compared the two responses, the more one question kept coming back:

Why does ChatGPT feel smarter than the OpenAI API, even when both use the same underlying model?

That question sounds simple.

The answer, however, has very little to do with GPT itself.

Instead, it has everything to do with architecture.

I Was Comparing Two Completely Different Products

The biggest mistake I made was assuming that ChatGPT and the OpenAI API were the same product.

They aren’t.

They’re built for entirely different audiences.

ChatGPT is designed for people who simply want an intelligent assistant.

The OpenAI API is designed for developers who want to build intelligent assistants.

That distinction sounds subtle, but it changes everything.

Think about buying a car.

One option is purchasing a fully assembled Tesla that’s ready to drive.

The other is purchasing only the electric motor.

Both use incredible technology.

But one already has navigation, safety systems, sensors, software, and a polished driving experience.

The other gives you the freedom to build your own vehicle.

That’s exactly the relationship between ChatGPT and the API.

ChatGPT Is Much More Than Just GPT

I used to imagine ChatGPT working like this:

Me
 ↓
GPT
 ↓
Answer

But after digging deeper, I realized the real flow is much richer.

User
   │
   ▼
Request Router
   │
   ▼
Should I search the web?
Should I use memory?
Should I analyze files?
Should I call another tool?
   │
   ▼
Context Builder
   │
   ▼
GPT Model
   │
   ▼
Post Processing
   │
   ▼
Final Response

Suddenly, everything made sense.

Before the language model even starts generating words, an entire orchestration layer decides how the request should be handled.

That orchestration is what makes ChatGPT feel intelligent.

The model is only one component.

Then I Looked at the API

When I switched back to my application, the architecture looked completely different.

My Application
      │
      ▼
Prompt
      │
      ▼
GPT Model
      │
      ▼
Response

That’s it.

No automatic search.

No memory.

No context management.

No routing.

No orchestration.

And then it hit me.

The API isn’t missing features.

It’s waiting for me to build them.

Why Web Search Feels So Magical

The moment that impressed me most was watching ChatGPT decide to search the internet without me explicitly asking it to.

I wasn’t thinking,

“Search the web first.”

I simply asked a question.

ChatGPT made that decision on its own.

That means there’s another intelligent layer sitting above the model.

It evaluates questions like:

  • Is this information recent?
  • Do I need live sources?
  • Should I retrieve documents?
  • Should I use another tool before answering?

Only then does it invoke GPT.

With the API, none of this happens automatically.

If I want that experience, I have to build it myself.

That usually means integrating search providers, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), vector databases, prompt orchestration, and business logic.

In other words, I have to recreate the system that ChatGPT already provides.

The Real Intelligence Isn’t Just the Model

This realization changed how I evaluate AI products.

For months, I had been comparing language models.

Now I found myself comparing systems.

A great AI experience isn’t created by a powerful model alone.

It’s created by how well that model is surrounded by supporting components.

Memory.

Search.

Context management.

Tool selection.

Reasoning orchestration.

Safety layers.

Conversation history.

All of these pieces work together before the model even begins writing.

The model is the brain.

The surrounding architecture is the nervous system.

Without that system, the brain can’t reach its full potential.

Why OpenAI Keeps Them Separate

Initially, I wondered why OpenAI didn’t simply expose every ChatGPT feature through the API.

But after thinking about it, the separation makes perfect sense.

Imagine if every application were forced to use ChatGPT’s workflow.

Developers would lose flexibility.

Some applications don’t need web search.

Others require proprietary databases.

Some must follow strict business rules.

Others need custom workflows or domain-specific tools.

The API provides raw capability.

ChatGPT provides a finished experience.

One is a platform for builders.

The other is a product for users.

Neither is better.

They’re solving different problems.

My Biggest Takeaway

The biggest lesson I learned wasn’t about GPT.

It was about software architecture.

When people say,

“ChatGPT is smarter than the API,”

they’re usually comparing an entire ecosystem with a single building block.

That’s not a fair comparison.

The intelligence isn’t only inside the language model.

It’s inside the routing.

The search.

The orchestration.

The memory.

The context.

And all the engineering built around it.

Once I understood that, something clicked.

I stopped trying to make the API behave exactly like ChatGPT.

Instead, I started asking a better question:

What architecture do I need to build to create the experience my users actually need?

Ironically, that question turned out to be far more valuable than the one I started with.

articles.title: Building a Full Stack Language Translation Website. Part-1
articles.author: Dedipya Goswami
articles.description: Welcome to the world of full stack development, where we’ll explore the intricacies of building a language translation website from the ground 0. In this blog ...
articles.content:
Welcome to the world of full stack development, where we’ll explore the intricacies of building a language translation website from the ground 0. In this blog post, I’ll walk you through the technical stack I used to create a powerful platform that enables seamless translation between multiple languages and later how i built the website.

Tech Stack Overview :

  • Frontend: HTML , CSS , JS , Bootstrap
  • Backend : Node.js , Express.js , Python , FastAPI
  • Database : MySQL
  • Transliteration Services : Gemini API

Here’s an Level 1 DFD for the Full Stack application that i have created :

In this blog post i will share how i built the backend for the Website using FastAPI.

To start, I attempted to build a standard Python code that utilizes Facebook’s mBART-50, a many-to-many multilingual model, for machine translation. This came after several attempts on my part to train a language translation model using the IIT Bombay Corpus Dataset.

This is the code :

from transformers import MBartForConditionalGeneration, MBart50TokenizerFast
import torch


model = MBartForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained("facebook/mbart-large-50-one-to-many-mmt")
tokenizer = MBart50TokenizerFast.from_pretrained("facebook/mbart-large-50-one-to-many-mmt", src_lang="en_XX")

# Mapping wrt to MBart 

language_mapping = {
    "arabic": "ar_AR",
    "english": "en_XX",
    "gujarati": "gu_IN",
    "hindi": "hi_IN",
    "bengali": "bn_IN",
    "malayalam": "ml_IN",
    "marathi": "mr_IN",
    "tamil": "ta_IN",
    "telugu": "te_IN"
}

def translate(articles_en, target_lang, batch_size=4):
    num_articles = len(articles_en)
    translations = []

    for i in range(0, num_articles, batch_size):
        batch_articles = articles_en[i:i+batch_size]
        model_inputs = tokenizer(batch_articles, return_tensors="pt", padding=True, truncation=True)
        target_lang_code = tokenizer.lang_code_to_id[target_lang]  # Use original case
        generated_tokens = model.generate(**model_inputs, forced_bos_token_id=target_lang_code)
        batch_translations = tokenizer.batch_decode(generated_tokens, skip_special_tokens=True)
        translations.extend(batch_translations)

    return translations

while True:
    x = input("Enter an article (type 'exit' to quit): ")
    if x.lower() == 'exit':
        break
    target_language = input("Enter the language for translation: ").lower()
    if target_language not in language_mapping:
        print("Invalid language name.")
        continue
    target_language_code = language_mapping[target_language]

    if len(x) > 512:  
        chunks = [x[i:i+512] for i in range(0, len(x), 512)]
        translations = translate(chunks, target_language_code)
    else:
        translations = translate([x], target_language_code)
    for translation in translations:
        print(translation)




data_to_pickle = {
    "translate_function": translate,
    "language_mapping": language_mapping
}

pickle_file_path = "translation_functions.pickle"


with open(pickle_file_path, "wb") as pickle_file:
    pickle.dump(data_to_pickle, pickle_file)

print("Pickle file has been created successfully:", pickle_file_path)

It loads the pre-trained mBART-50 model and tokenizer using MBartForConditionalGeneration and MBart50TokenizerFast from the Transformers library. These are initialized for translation from English to various languages.

A dictionary named language_mapping is defined to map language names to their respective language codes supported by the tokenizer.

Following that, there’s a translation function named translate. This function takes English articles and a target language as input and translates them accordingly. It operates by tokenizing input articles, generating translations using the model, and decoding the generated tokens. The translations are collected and returned.

The code enters a loop for user interaction. It prompts the user to input an article for translation and the target language. If the input is “exit”, the loop breaks; otherwise, it continues to translate the input text. If the input exceeds 512 tokens, it is split into manageable chunks for translation.

After this, I wanted to make an API so that i can use that API that accepts requests from my frontend and returns the response that i can render on to the Website. So i opted for FastAPI which is a python library used for making robust and light weighted APIs.

I named this file as app.py. And here it is :

from fastapi import FastAPI, File, UploadFile, HTTPException
from fastapi.middleware.cors import CORSMiddleware
from typing import List
from transformers import MBartForConditionalGeneration, MBart50TokenizerFast
import requests
import base64
import os
from dotenv import load_dotenv
from schemas import Text
from translation import translate_text
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI()

app.add_middleware(
    CORSMiddleware,
    allow_origins=["*"],
    allow_credentials=True,
    allow_methods=["*"],
    allow_headers=["*"]
)

load_dotenv()

Uptill here, the code sets up a FastAPI application to handle translation requests. It imports necessary modules such as FastAPI, Transformers for translation, requests for making HTTP requests, base64 for encoding and decoding data, os for interacting with the operating system, dotenv for loading environment variables, and Pydantic for creating data models.

After initializing the FastAPI application, it adds CORS middleware to enable Cross-Origin Resource Sharing, allowing requests from any origin with credentials, methods, and headers.

Environment variables are loaded using load_dotenv() to ensure secure configuration.

model = MBartForConditionalGeneration.from_pretrained("facebook/mbart-large-50-one-to-many-mmt")
tokenizer = MBart50TokenizerFast.from_pretrained("facebook/mbart-large-50-one-to-many-mmt", src_lang="en_XX")
language_mapping = {
    "arabic": "ar_AR",
    "english": "en_XX",
    "gujarati": "gu_IN",
    "hindi": "hi_IN",
    "bengali": "bn_IN",
    "malayalam": "ml_IN",
    "marathi": "mr_IN",
    "tamil": "ta_IN",
    "telugu": "te_IN"
}

Including the model and the language_mapping.

@app.get("/")
def index():
    return {"message": "Welcome to the translation API!"}

@app.post("/translate/")
async def translate_text_endpoint(Data: Text) -> List[str]:
    # Check if the target and source languages are supported
    if Data.target_language.lower() not in language_mapping or Data.source_language.lower() not in language_mapping:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=400, detail="Source or target language is not supported.")

    source_language_code = language_mapping[Data.source_language.lower()]
    target_language_code = language_mapping[Data.target_language.lower()]

    translations = translate_text([Data.text], source_language_code, target_language_code)

    return translations

The script defines two endpoints for the FastAPI application:

  1. Index Endpoint:
  • The index function is bound to the root URL ("/").
  • It returns a simple JSON response with a welcome message when the root URL is accessed. It is written for testing that whether the endpoint is working or not.

2. Translation Endpoint:

  • The translate_text_endpoint function is bound to the "/translate/" endpoint and expects a POST request with JSON data in the body conforming to the Text schema.
  • It first checks if the source and target languages specified in the request are supported by verifying them against the language_mapping dictionary. If not supported, it raises an HTTPException with a status code of 400 (Bad Request) and a corresponding error message.
  • If the languages are supported, it retrieves the language codes from the language_mapping dictionary.
  • It then calls the translate_text function with the input text, source language code, and target language/ code to perform the translation.
  • Finally, it returns the translated text as a list of strings.

Now what is the Text Schema ?

The Text schema is a Pydantic model used to define the structure of the JSON data expected in the request body for the translation endpoint. It helps in validating and parsing the incoming data into a Python object. It is defined in schemas.py.

schemas.py :

from pydantic import BaseModel

class Text(BaseModel):
    text: str
    source_language: str
    target_language: str

Now, the API creation is complete. It is accessible at “/translate/” endpoint of the localhost. For example : https://localhost:8000/translate/.

It can be tested as a part of White Box testing concept of Software Engineering in Postman or Thunder Client.

It can be used to render the response to the user request in the Frontend by a Javascript script like this :

const requestBody = {
      text: inputText,
      source_language: inputLanguage,
      target_language: outputLanguage,
    };

    try {
      const response = await fetch("http://localhost:8000/translate/", {
        method: "POST",
        headers: {
          "Content-Type": "application/json",
        },
        body: JSON.stringify(requestBody),
      });

      if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error("Translation request failed.");
      }

      const translatedText = await response.json();
      document.getElementById("output-text").textContent = translatedText[0];

In this way, I have build a frontend for the website and then in this way for the Text Translation module, i have build the Backend , handling the request-response communication between the client and server for the website.

My project also has a PDF Translational Module, which accepts a PDF document from the user and translates the PDF into the target language requested by the User. About this will be written in the part 2 of the blog.

U can find the GitHub repository dedicated for this project here.

P.S: This was my first ever blog that i wrote. So if u find this helpful, please give a like and do read the next part of the blog.
